tagline: The Nature Island of the Caribbean
overview:
Dominica is a rugged volcanic island in the eastern Caribbean, lying between the French islands of Guadeloupe and Martinique. It is often confused with the much larger Dominican Republic, but the two are very different places. Dominica covers about 750 km², a little smaller than New York City, and only about 70,000 people live there, most of them along the coast around the capital, Roseau.

Islanders call it the Nature Island, and the name fits. Steep green mountains, some of them still-active volcanoes, rise straight from the sea, and rainforest covers most of the interior. Instead of white sand and big resorts, Dominica offers hot springs, waterfalls, hiking trails and whales offshore.

Dominica is also home to the Kalinago, the last remaining community of the Caribbean's original Indigenous people, who live on their own territory on the east coast. English is the official language, and many people also speak a French-based Creole. The country is an independent republic in the Commonwealth with an elected parliament and president.
landAndNature:
Dominica is one of the youngest and most mountainous islands in the Caribbean, with nine volcanoes packed into a small space; Morne Diablotins, the highest, reaches about 1,450 meters. Rain falls almost daily on the peaks, feeding so many streams that islanders say there is one river for each day of the year. In the Morne Trois Pitons National Park, a World Heritage Site, the Boiling Lake bubbles at close to 90 degrees Celsius, the second-largest hot lake in the world, and the Valley of Desolation hisses with steam vents.

Hurricanes are the great danger; Hurricane Maria in 2017 damaged nearly every building on the island. The forests shelter the sisserou parrot, a large purple-and-green bird found nowhere else and shown on the national flag. Sperm whales live in the deep waters offshore all year, and Champagne Reef fizzes with volcanic bubbles.
peopleAndCulture:
Most Dominicans are of African descent, with about 3,000 Kalinago people living in the Kalinago Territory, where they weave baskets and build traditional canoes. English is spoken in schools and government, while Kwéyòl, a Creole related to French, is heard in markets and songs. Creole Day in October celebrates the language with traditional dress in bright madras plaid.

Food centers on root vegetables, plantains, fresh fish and callaloo, a thick green soup, along with bakes, fried dough eaten for breakfast. The World Creole Music Festival each October fills Roseau with bouyon, zouk and reggae. Cricket is the favorite sport, and the Waitukubuli National Trail, about 185 kilometers long, lets hikers cross the whole island. Independence celebrations in November include a heritage day honoring the island's villages.
history:
The Kalinago, whom Europeans called Caribs, arrived from South America and named the island Waitukubuli, "tall is her body." Columbus sighted it on a Sunday in November 1493 and called it Dominica, Latin for Sunday. Its steep terrain and fierce defenders kept Europeans away longer than on other islands.

France and Britain fought over Dominica through the 1700s, and Britain won it for good in 1783. Enslaved Africans worked coffee and sugar plantations until slavery was abolished in 1834, and in 1838 Dominica became the only British Caribbean colony with a legislature controlled by Black members. The island joined the West Indies Federation in the 1950s and became independent on November 3, 1978. Hurricanes David in 1979 and Maria in 2017 caused huge damage, and the country now aims to become the world's first fully climate-resilient nation.
funFacts: The sisserou parrot on Dominica's flag makes it one of only a couple of national flags that use the color purple.
Dominica's Boiling Lake is about 60 meters across and so hot that its center is a constant rolling boil.
The Kalinago Territory in Dominica is the only remaining Indigenous community of its kind in the Caribbean.
Parts of the Pirates of the Caribbean films were shot in Dominica's rivers and forests.
The island has around 365 rivers, one for every day of the year, according to local tradition.
Sperm whales can be seen off Dominica in every month of the year, which is rare anywhere in the world.
